nameStory: The name 'Siberian Burnet' reflects this plant's Asian origins and its membership in the burnet family. 'Burnet' comes from the Old French 'brunette,' meaning 'little brown one,' referring to the brownish flower heads that develop after blooming. The scientific name Sanguisorba means 'blood-absorber,' as these plants were historically used to stop bleeding.
description: Siberian Burnet is a graceful perennial herb that grows 2-4 feet tall with an upright, branching habit. It produces distinctive bottlebrush-like flower spikes that are white to pale pink and droop elegantly from slender stems. The compound leaves are divided into many small, toothed leaflets that give the plant a delicate, fern-like appearance. As a member of the rose family, it shares characteristics with roses and strawberries, though it looks quite different from its more familiar relatives.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Drooping, cylindrical flower spikes 1-3 inches long that look like fuzzy white or pale pink bottlebrushes. The flowers lack petals - what you see are actually prominent white stamens (male flower parts) that give the spike its fluffy appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves divided into 7-17 oval leaflets with sharp teeth along the edges. The leaflets feel smooth and somewhat thin, and are arranged in pairs along the leaf stem with one terminal leaflet at the tip.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright perennial that forms clumps 2-4 feet tall. The stems are smooth, branching in the upper portions, and feel firm but not woody when squeezed gently.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry, four-angled fruits develop after flowering, enclosed by the persistent sepals (outer flower parts). The fruiting spikes turn brown and remain on the plant into winter.

habitat: **Note: This identification is uncertain given the extremely limited observation data.** Siberian Burnet typically grows in moist meadows, along stream banks, and in other wet or seasonally moist areas. In its native range, it prefers rich, organic soils and can tolerate partial shade, though the specific habitat preferences in New England are unclear due to its rarity here.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as clusters of compound leaves. Young foliage is bright green and the leaflets unfurl gradually from the base of the plant upward.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from mid to late summer, when the distinctive drooping white flower spikes appear. This is the best time for identification when the bottlebrush flowers are most prominent.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and develop into brown fruiting spikes. Leaves may begin to yellow, and the dried flower heads become more noticeable as other vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back in cold climates. Dried stems and persistent fruiting spikes may remain visible, appearing as brown, cylindrical structures on brittle stalks.

funFact: Despite being called 'Siberian' Burnet, this plant's drooping flower spikes actually inspired traditional Japanese floral arrangements, where it's prized for its elegant, cascading form that resembles flowing water frozen in time.
confusionNotes: The drooping, bottlebrush-like flowers distinguish Siberian Burnet from its relatives - Canadian Burnet has upright white spikes, while Great Burnet has upright reddish-purple flower heads. Remember: 'Siberian droops, the others stand up straight.'
contextualKnowledge: **Important note: This species has only been recorded once in New England, making field identification uncertain.** Siberian Burnet may be an escaped garden plant or a misidentified specimen. If you think you've found this species, documentation with photos and expert verification would be valuable for regional botanical records.
compareHints: Siberian Burnet is the only burnet in New England with drooping flower spikes - all other burnets have upright flower heads. Canadian Burnet is much taller (up to 6 feet) with upright white spikes, Great Burnet has dark red-purple upright heads, and Salad Burnet is much shorter with rounded pinkish-green flower heads. The drooping habit makes Siberian Burnet unmistakable among its genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canadian burnet is the tallest burnet species you'll find in New England, easily distinguished from its relatives by its creamy white flowers (great burnet has dark red flowers, while salad burnet has tiny greenish flowers with red tips).
Great burnet towers over its relatives, reaching 3-6 feet compared to Canadian burnet's 2-4 feet and salad burnet's modest 1-2 feet.
Unlike its relatives Canadian burnet and great burnet which are native and have white or pink flowers, salad burnet has those distinctive dark crimson flower heads and is much smaller overall.
